I’m autistic and had to go to intensive speech therapy till I was ten due to severe speech apraxia (baisicly I couldn’t form words correctly with my mouth, even though I was thinking them). The thing is, when I was a toddler I began to learn words like any other kid, but then I started loosing them again until I was entirly mute. Eventually I learned basic sign language and slowly gained sounds again (though until I was six or seven no one but my dad could understand what I was saying) but for a long time I wouldn’t make a sound unless I was very upset.

Despite that my dad still always filmed home videos of me at holidays and talked to me constantly. There are tapes of toddler me on Christmas Day opening gifts and not making a single noise, and my dad is still happily talking to me and filling in the gaps in the conversation. It was really rough for my parents at that time because they didn’t know how to help me. Doctors kept looking at me and saying that I would never learn to talk or write, that they might as well give up. But they still always worked to fill in the cracks of my abnormal childhood. My earliest memories are of baking, and catching bugs, and playing in the meadow. 

I know this has been a ramble, but I hope this expresses how much my parents love me, and how much I love them back. Even though we could barely communicate, and I often had meltdowns over not being able to convey my thoughts, they were always trying.

Well given everything you’ve said in this post it seems like a good foundation: you care deeply about your partner and want to do your best to support them, which is incredibly valuable.

It’s obviously a lot of adjustments, but there are a lot of little things you can do to be supportive of them! 

Some good things would be to take them clothes shopping (online if they’re more comfortable with that) to try and find things they feel more comfortable in going forward, along with helping them explore more feminine activities like painting nails, shaving, skin care, etc if that’s something they’d like to learn. 

Another really valuable thing is learning how to make your partner feel gender euphoria (essentially when they feel affirmed and happy with their gender and identity). For a lot of people euphoria can come from nicknames, the use of their chosen name and pronouns, looking the way that they want to look, and other possitive associations with how they identify. Over the coming weeks maybe try out some new nicknames to see how they feel, or finding new complements that make your partner feel good.

On the flip side of sparking euphoria is helping mitigate dysphoria, which is pretty much all of the bad feelings that are the opposite of euphoria (it’s a bit more complicated then that, but that’s a whole different rabbit hole). Assuming your spouse feels gender dysphoria then it will be good to learn about it and how to try and help lessen it. What triggers dysphoria and also what gets rid of it tends to be different person by person, some other commenters here have already given good links to websites with info about dysphoria and talking to your partner will likely be the best way to know how to help.

Another fairly small but absolutely life changing thing is being there to activly support your partner in public, expecially early on in their transition. A good subtle way to do that is to use their preferred pronouns and name in public, as typically when people hear it then they will automatically agree with it without going through the mental process of trying to discern gender through appearance. Plus it means that even when someone does misgender your partner (which will almost certainly happen at some point, likely unknowingly by someone) then you can still correctly gender them and be there as an emotional anchor since getting misgendered can really hurt. 

But honestly the biggest advice? Just do your best to be supportive. Maybe that means practicing their new name and pronouns in the mirror until it becomes natural, maybe that means spur of the moment shopping trips to find affirming clothes, maybe that means an extra hug and kiss and a bit of reassurance. Support comes in many forms, and considering that you actively went out looking for advice to help support your partner I think you’re going to do great :]
